summary: This unit covers chronic inflammatory skin disease: rosacea, lichen planus, and psoriasis, plus pyoderma gangrenosum, hidradenitis suppurativa, and the alopecias. The exam gives you a lesion and where it sits, and asks for the immune mechanism, the histology, or the disease it travels with.

points: Adults (often 30 to 50) with central facial flushing, persistent erythema, and telangiectasias on cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead.
Papules and pustules can appear, but there are no comedones.
Triggers cause flushing: heat, sunlight, alcohol, spicy food, hot drinks, and emotional stress.
Complications: rhinophyma (bulbous nose from sebaceous and fibrous overgrowth) and ocular rosacea (blepharitis, conjunctivitis, gritty eyes).

Look-alikes: acne vulgaris has comedones in teens; seborrheic dermatitis has greasy yellow scale in nasolabial folds, brows, and scalp; the lupus malar rash spares the nasolabial folds and comes with systemic findings.
notes.why: Rosacea reflects neurovascular dysregulation plus innate immune activation in central facial skin. Triggers such as heat, alcohol, and spicy food activate sensory channels such as TRPV1, which release vasoactive neuropeptides and cause flushing; repeated vasodilation leaves fixed erythema and telangiectasias. The protease kallikrein 5 cleaves excess cathelicidin into active peptides such as LL-37, which drive inflammation and new vessel growth, producing papules and pustules. The process is not centered on a plugged follicle, so comedones are absent, and years of inflammation drive the sebaceous and fibrous overgrowth of rhinophyma.

points: The 6 Ps: pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules and plaques, often on flexor wrists, shins, and genitals.
Wickham striae: fine white lines on the surface of the papules.
Oral lesions: white lacy (reticular) network on the buccal mucosa.
Histology: band-like T cell infiltrate along the dermal-epidermal junction, sawtooth rete ridges, hypergranulosis, and Civatte (colloid) bodies, which are apoptotic basal keratinocytes.
Mechanism: cytotoxic CD8 T cells attack basal keratinocytes.
Linked to hepatitis C infection.
notes.why: Lichen planus is an interface dermatitis: CD8 cytotoxic T cells collect in a band at the dermal-epidermal junction and kill basal keratinocytes by apoptosis. The dead basal cells become Civatte bodies, and the damaged basal layer gives the junction its sawtooth outline. The overlying epidermis responds with a thickened granular layer (hypergranulosis), which shows on the surface as Wickham striae. The violaceous color comes from the dense infiltrate plus melanin that falls into the dermis when basal cells die (pigment incontinence).

points: Dendritic cells make IL-23, which expands Th17 cells; IL-17 and TNF drive keratinocyte hyperproliferation and neutrophil recruitment.
Strong genetic risk; HLA-Cw6 is the classic allele.
Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery scale on elbows, knees, scalp, and lumbosacral skin.
Koebner phenomenon: new plaques form at sites of skin trauma.
Nails: pitting, onycholysis, and oil-drop discoloration; nail disease raises the odds of psoriatic arthritis (DIP joints, dactylitis, pencil-in-cup deformity).

Histology: acanthosis with regular elongation of rete ridges, parakeratosis, thin or absent granular layer, thin suprapapillary plates over dilated capillaries, and Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in the stratum corneum).
Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding when scale is lifted, because only a thin plate of epidermis covers the dilated papillary capillaries.
notes.why: An IL-23 to Th17 loop keeps psoriatic keratinocytes cycling fast: IL-17 and IL-22 drive proliferation, and the keratinocytes release chemokines and antimicrobial peptides that recruit more neutrophils and T cells. Epidermal transit time falls from about a month to a few days, so cells reach the surface with nuclei still present (parakeratosis) and the granular layer never forms properly. Neutrophils migrate into the scale as Munro microabscesses, and dilated papillary capillaries under a thin suprapapillary plate explain the pinpoint bleeding of the Auspitz sign.

points: Pyoderma gangrenosum: neutrophilic dermatosis, not an infection; painful ulcer with a violaceous, undermined border, often on the legs.
Pathergy: trauma or surgical debridement makes it worse.
Associations: inflammatory bowel disease (especially ulcerative colitis), rheumatoid arthritis, and hematologic malignancy.
Hidradenitis suppurativa: chronic follicular occlusion in the axillae, groin, and perineum, with painful nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts, and rope-like scars.
Hidradenitis risk factors: obesity and smoking; onset after puberty.
notes.why: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a disorder of excessive neutrophil activation driven by cytokines such as IL-1, IL-8, and TNF, with no microbe involved, so cultures are negative and cutting into the lesion recruits more neutrophils (pathergy). The same dysregulated innate immunity links it to IBD, rheumatoid arthritis, and myeloid disorders. Hidradenitis suppurativa starts with hyperkeratotic plugging of the hair follicle in skin folds; the plugged follicle dilates and ruptures, spilling keratin and bacteria into the dermis, which drives abscesses and epithelium-lined sinus tracts. Friction, obesity, and smoking promote this follicular occlusion, which is why it favors the axillae and groin after puberty.

points: Nonscarring alopecia keeps the follicle openings, so hair can regrow; scarring alopecia destroys follicles and leaves smooth skin with no openings.
Alopecia areata: autoimmune T cell attack on anagen follicles; round smooth patches with exclamation point hairs (tapered toward the scalp).
Androgenetic alopecia: DHT (from 5-alpha reductase) miniaturizes follicles; vertex and frontotemporal thinning in men, widened central part in women.
Telogen effluvium: a stressor (childbirth, surgery, high fever, crash diet) shifts many follicles into telogen; diffuse shedding of club hairs about 2 to 4 months later.
Scarring alopecia: lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus, and other inflammation that destroys the follicle stem cells.
notes.why: Hair follicles cycle through anagen (growth), catagen (involution), and telogen (rest), and each type of hair loss disrupts a different part of this cycle. In alopecia areata the anagen bulb loses its normal immune privilege, so autoreactive CD8 T cells attack it; the shaft narrows and breaks near the scalp (exclamation point hair), but the bulge stem cells survive, so regrowth is possible. DHT shortens anagen and miniaturizes androgen-sensitive scalp follicles, and telogen effluvium pushes many follicles into telogen at once, so shedding appears about 3 months later when telogen ends. Scarring alopecia destroys the bulge stem cells, so the loss is permanent.

tricks.label: The 6 Ps of lichen planus
tricks.text: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar, Papules, Plaques.

tricks.label: Psoriasis sits outside, eczema sits inside
tricks.text: Adult psoriasis favors extensor surfaces (elbows, knees). Adult atopic dermatitis favors flexures (antecubital and popliteal fossae).

tricks.label: Comedones decide acne versus rosacea
tricks.text: Pustules on the face with blackheads or whiteheads point to acne vulgaris. Pustules with flushing and telangiectasias but no comedones point to rosacea.

highYield: Facial flushing after wine and hot coffee, telangiectasias, pustules, no comedones: rosacea; may progress to rhinophyma.
Itchy purple flat-topped papules on the wrists with lacy white buccal lesions: lichen planus; screen for hepatitis C.
Psoriasis is driven by IL-23 and IL-17 from Th17 cells, with TNF as a key cytokine.
Munro microabscesses and the Auspitz sign are psoriasis clues; nail pitting predicts psoriatic arthritis.
Painful ulcer with a purple undermined edge that worsens after debridement in a patient with ulcerative colitis: pyoderma gangrenosum.
Recurrent painful axillary and groin nodules with sinus tracts in a smoker with obesity: hidradenitis suppurativa.
Exclamation point hairs in a smooth round patch: alopecia areata.
pitfalls: Lupus malar rash spares the nasolabial folds; seborrheic dermatitis involves them with greasy scale; rosacea has telangiectasias and pustules.
Koebner phenomenon is seen in both psoriasis and lichen planus, so use the lesion color and scale to separate them.
Pyoderma gangrenosum looks infected, but cultures are negative and debridement makes it worse.
Telogen effluvium starts months after the trigger, so ask about events 2 to 4 months back.

flows.title: Psoriasis pathogenesis
steps: Genetic risk (HLA-Cw6) plus a trigger activates dermal dendritic cells
Dendritic cells secrete IL-23 and TNF
IL-23 expands and sustains Th17 cells
IL-17 and IL-22 drive keratinocyte proliferation and chemokine release
Fast turnover causes acanthosis, parakeratosis, and loss of the granular layer
Recruited neutrophils collect in the stratum corneum as Munro microabscesses

flows.title: Lichen planus pathogenesis
steps: CD8 cytotoxic T cells target an antigen on basal keratinocytes
T cells form a band along the dermal-epidermal junction
T cells trigger apoptosis of basal keratinocytes
Dead basal cells form Civatte bodies; the junction becomes sawtoothed
Melanin drops into the dermis and the granular layer thickens
Result: violaceous polygonal papules with Wickham striae

summary: Blistering diseases come from a broken adhesion protein, either from a gene defect (epidermolysis bullosa) or from autoantibodies (pemphigus, pemphigoid, dermatitis herpetiformis). The exam asks you to match the target protein to the split level, the Nikolsky sign, the mouth findings, and the immunofluorescence pattern.

points: Desmosomes join keratinocytes to each other; their cadherins are desmoglein 1 and desmoglein 3.
Desmoglein 3 is concentrated in the lower epidermis and in mucosa; desmoglein 1 is concentrated in the upper epidermis.
Hemidesmosomes anchor basal cells to the basement membrane through BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230.
Below the basal cell: lamina lucida (laminin 332), lamina densa (type IV collagen), then anchoring fibrils (type VII collagen) into the dermis.
The deeper the split, the more tense the blister and the more likely scarring.
notes.why: Each adhesion protein sits at a specific depth, so the protein that is attacked or missing predicts the level of the split and the clinical picture. A split inside the epidermis leaves a thin, fragile roof that ruptures easily (flaccid blister), while a split beneath the whole epidermis keeps a full-thickness roof that stays tense. Desmoglein compensation explains where blisters appear: mucosa relies mainly on desmoglein 3 and the superficial epidermis mainly on desmoglein 1, so each site blisters when its dominant desmoglein is lost. Splits at or below the lamina densa injure the dermis and heal with scarring.

points: Inherited defects in adhesion proteins; blisters from minor friction starting at birth or infancy; mouth and nails are often involved.
Simplex: keratins 5 and 14; basal keratinocytes break; usually heals without scarring.
Junctional: laminin 332 or collagen XVII; split in the lamina lucida; severe forms can be fatal in infancy.
Dystrophic: type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils); split below the lamina densa.
Recessive dystrophic: heavy scarring, fused digits (mitten hands), nail loss, esophageal strictures, and aggressive squamous cell carcinoma in young adults.
notes.why: Epidermolysis bullosa shows that losing a structural protein places the blister at that protein's level. Keratins 5 and 14 form the intermediate filament scaffold of basal cells, so mutations make basal cells burst under friction, and the split heals without scarring. Laminin 332 and collagen XVII link the hemidesmosome to the lamina densa, so junctional disease splits in the lamina lucida. Type VII collagen forms anchoring fibrils, so dystrophic disease splits below the lamina densa, and repeated dermal wounding and scarring cause mitten hands, strictures, and aggressive squamous cell carcinoma in chronic wounds.

points: Type II hypersensitivity: IgG against desmogleins causes acantholysis (keratinocytes fall apart).
Pemphigus vulgaris: anti-desmoglein 3 (often also 1); suprabasal split; basal cells stay attached like a row of tombstones.
Painful oral erosions usually come first, then flaccid bullae that rupture easily.
Nikolsky sign positive: gentle pressure shears off the epidermis.
Direct immunofluorescence: net-like (fishnet) IgG around keratinocytes.
Pemphigus foliaceus: anti-desmoglein 1 only; subcorneal split near the granular layer; scaly crusted erosions; no mucosal lesions.
notes.why: In pemphigus, IgG autoantibodies bind desmogleins and directly disrupt desmosome adhesion, a type II mechanism that does not need complement, so keratinocytes round up and separate (acantholysis). Desmoglein 3 dominates in mucosa and the lower epidermis, so anti-desmoglein 3 antibody causes oral erosions first and a suprabasal split, while hemidesmosomes keep the basal row attached like tombstones. Antibody coats the surface of every keratinocyte, which outlines each cell in a net pattern on immunofluorescence. The split is intraepidermal with a thin roof, so blisters are flaccid and the Nikolsky sign is positive.

points: IgG against BP180 and BP230 in hemidesmosomes; complement activation draws in eosinophils.
Older adults (usually over 60) with tense subepidermal bullae, often on flexures, trunk, and thighs, with itching.
Oral lesions are infrequent; Nikolsky sign negative.
Direct immunofluorescence: linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane.
notes.why: In bullous pemphigoid, IgG binds BP180 and BP230 at the hemidesmosome and activates complement. Complement fragments recruit eosinophils and neutrophils, and their proteases detach the basal cells from the basement membrane. The split is subepidermal, so the entire epidermis forms the roof, which keeps the bullae tense and the Nikolsky sign negative. Antibody and C3 lie in a continuous line along the basement membrane, which gives the linear immunofluorescence pattern.

points: IgA against epidermal transglutaminase, tied to celiac disease (gluten sensitivity).
Grouped, very itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces: elbows, knees, buttocks, upper back.
Histology: neutrophilic microabscesses at the tips of dermal papillae.
Direct immunofluorescence: granular IgA in the dermal papillae.
notes.why: In people with HLA-DQ2 or DQ8, gluten exposure drives IgA against tissue transglutaminase in the gut and then against epidermal transglutaminase (TG3). IgA bound to TG3 deposits in the tips of the dermal papillae, where it draws in neutrophils that form papillary microabscesses and lift the epidermis into small subepidermal vesicles. Because the deposits sit as clumps in the papillae, direct immunofluorescence is granular, and a gluten-free diet removes the antigen that drives the disease.

charts.title: Epidermolysis bullosa types
rows: Friction blisters, usually heal without scars
Can be severe and fatal in infancy

tricks.label: Vulgaris starts in the mouth
tricks.text: Desmoglein 3 dominates in mucosa, so pemphigus vulgaris hits the mouth first. Foliaceus targets only desmoglein 1, which mucosa does not depend on, so the mouth is spared.

tricks.label: Tense means deep
tricks.text: A blister with a full epidermal roof (pemphigoid) stays tense. A blister with only part of the epidermis as its roof (pemphigus) is flaccid and ruptures.

tricks.label: Fishnet versus single line
tricks.text: Antibody between every keratinocyte draws a net: pemphigus. Antibody along one line at the base draws a single line: pemphigoid.

highYield: Middle-aged adult with painful oral erosions, then flaccid bullae and a positive Nikolsky sign: pemphigus vulgaris (anti-desmoglein 3).
Older adult with itchy tense bullae and negative Nikolsky sign: bullous pemphigoid (anti-BP180 and BP230).
Eosinophils in a subepidermal blister point to bullous pemphigoid.
Grouped itchy vesicles on the elbows with chronic diarrhea: dermatitis herpetiformis and celiac disease.
Recessive dystrophic EB: type VII collagen defect, mitten hands, and early squamous cell carcinoma.
EB simplex: keratin 5 and 14 mutation; split within basal cells.
pitfalls: Pemphigus is intraepidermal and Nikolsky positive; pemphigoid is subepidermal and Nikolsky negative.
Pemphigus foliaceus and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome both cut desmoglein 1, one by IgG and one by bacterial toxin.
Linear IgG at the basement membrane means pemphigoid; granular IgA at papillary tips means dermatitis herpetiformis.
EB is inherited and starts at birth; the autoimmune blistering diseases start later in life.

dumps.p: Draw two keratinocytes resting on the basement membrane above the dermis. Label the adhesion proteins, then mark where each blistering disease splits the skin.
l: Desmosomes with desmoglein 1 (upper) and desmoglein 3 (lower and mucosa)
Hemidesmosomes with BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230
Lamina lucida with laminin 332, lamina densa, anchoring fibrils of type VII collagen
Pemphigus foliaceus: subcorneal split
Pemphigus vulgaris: suprabasal split
Bullous pemphigoid: subepidermal split
EB simplex in basal cells, junctional in lamina lucida, dystrophic below lamina densa

Dermatitis herpetiformis: epidermal transglutaminase, IgA

Fishnet IgG in pemphigus, linear IgG and C3 in pemphigoid

flows.title: Pemphigus vulgaris pathogenesis
steps: IgG autoantibodies form against desmoglein 3, often also desmoglein 1
IgG binds desmogleins on keratinocyte surfaces throughout the epidermis
Desmosome adhesion fails and keratinocytes separate (acantholysis)
The split forms just above the basal layer; basal cells stay anchored
The thin roof ruptures, leaving painful oral and skin erosions

flows.title: Bullous pemphigoid pathogenesis
steps: IgG autoantibodies bind BP180 and BP230 in basal cell hemidesmosomes
Bound IgG activates complement along the basement membrane
Complement fragments recruit eosinophils and neutrophils
Released proteases detach basal cells from the basement membrane
A subepidermal split forms tense bullae under an intact epidermis

flows.title: Dermatitis herpetiformis pathogenesis
steps: Gluten exposure in a person with HLA-DQ2 or DQ8
IgA forms against tissue transglutaminase, then epidermal transglutaminase
IgA deposits as granules in the tips of dermal papillae
Neutrophils gather into papillary microabscesses
Grouped, itchy subepidermal vesicles form on extensor surfaces

summary: This unit links two skin findings to their molecular defects: albinism (melanin cannot be made) and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (collagen is built or processed wrongly). The exam asks you to name the enzyme or collagen type, predict the complications, and separate these from Chediak-Higashi, Marfan, and osteogenesis imperfecta.

points: Autosomal recessive; melanocyte numbers are normal, but they cannot make melanin.
Classic form (OCA1): loss of tyrosinase, the enzyme that turns tyrosine into DOPA and on toward melanin; other forms lose melanosome proteins such as the OCA2 (P) protein.
Very pale skin, white or light hair, and light irises from birth.
No melanin shield, so sunburn, actinic damage, and squamous and basal cell carcinoma occur early.
Eyes: nystagmus, reduced visual acuity, photophobia, and strabismus from abnormal retinal and optic pathway development.
notes.why: Melanin is made inside melanosomes from tyrosine, and tyrosinase catalyzes the first steps (tyrosine to DOPA to dopaquinone). In OCA1 the enzyme is absent or inactive, so melanocytes are present but make little or no pigment; in OCA2 the P protein defect disturbs melanosome function and pigment output falls. Without melanin to absorb UV, keratinocyte DNA collects UV damage early, raising skin cancer risk. Melanin in the developing retina also guides optic nerve fibers, so its absence causes foveal hypoplasia and excess crossing at the optic chiasm, which explains the nystagmus, low acuity, and strabismus.

points: Ocular albinism: X-linked (affects boys); eyes are involved, skin is near normal.
Chediak-Higashi syndrome: autosomal recessive LYST defect in lysosomal trafficking.
Chediak-Higashi findings: partial albinism, giant granules in neutrophils, recurrent pyogenic (staphylococcal and streptococcal) infections, peripheral neuropathy, and bleeding.
Vitiligo differs: melanocytes are destroyed, so patches are depigmented in an acquired pattern.
notes.why: These disorders differ by where the defect sits. Ocular albinism is caused by loss of GPR143, a melanosome protein needed mainly in the eye, so the visual pathway is affected while skin pigment is near normal. In Chediak-Higashi syndrome, defective LYST disrupts trafficking of lysosomes and related organelles, so melanosomes clump (partial albinism), neutrophil granules fuse into giant granules that fail to fuse with phagosomes, and platelet dense granules are deficient. Vitiligo is acquired: autoreactive CD8 T cells destroy melanocytes, so the white patches have no melanocytes at all.

points: Collagen is a triple helix with glycine at every third position.
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases (vitamin C dependent) hydroxylate residues inside the cell.
Procollagen peptidases trim the ends outside the cell; lysyl oxidase (copper dependent) then cross-links fibrils.
Type I: skin, bone, tendon. Type III: blood vessels, bowel, uterus, granulation tissue. Type V: works with type I in skin.
notes.why: Glycine, the smallest amino acid, is the only residue that fits in the crowded center of the triple helix, so a glycine substitution distorts the whole molecule. Hydroxyproline forms hydrogen bonds that stabilize the helix, and hydroxylysine provides sites for glycosylation and later cross-links; both hydroxylases need vitamin C to keep their iron in the ferrous state, which is why scurvy causes fragile vessels and poor wound healing. Outside the cell, peptidases remove the propeptides so tropocollagen can assemble into fibrils, and copper-dependent lysyl oxidase forms covalent cross-links that give tensile strength.

points: Classic type: type V collagen (COL5A1); hyperextensible soft skin and joint hypermobility.
Vascular type: type III collagen (COL3A1), autosomal dominant; thin translucent skin with visible veins.
Vascular type risks: arterial rupture, bowel perforation, uterine rupture in pregnancy, and berry aneurysms.
Kyphoscoliotic type: lysyl hydroxylase deficiency, autosomal recessive; hypotonia, kyphoscoliosis, fragile sclerae.
Skin: fragile, bruises easily, heals with wide atrophic cigarette-paper scars.
Joints: hypermobility with recurrent dislocations.
notes.why: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a group of defects in collagen structure or processing, and the collagen type involved predicts which tissues fail. Type V collagen regulates the diameter of type I fibrils, so in classic EDS the fibrils are disorganized and weak, giving hyperextensible skin, lax joints, and wide atrophic scars. Type III collagen is a major fibrillar collagen of arterial walls, bowel, and uterus, so vascular EDS presents with rupture of these hollow organs. In the kyphoscoliotic type, lysyl hydroxylase deficiency prevents stable cross-links, weakening sclera, ligaments, and spinal support.

charts.title: Pigment disorders
rows: Tyrosinase or melanosome proteins (such as OCA2)
Pale skin, hair, and eyes; skin cancer; nystagmus, low acuity
Eye findings in boys, skin near normal
Partial albinism, giant granules, pyogenic infections, neuropathy

charts.title: Connective tissue disorders compared
rows: Hyperextensible fragile skin, cigarette-paper scars, hypermobility
Arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture; berry aneurysms
Lens subluxation, aortic root dilation and dissection
Repeated fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss, dental defects

tricks.label: Three for the vessels
tricks.text: Type III collagen is the vascular collagen, and loss of it gives the vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos with arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture.

tricks.label: Count versus color
tricks.text: Albinism has a normal melanocyte count with no pigment made. Vitiligo has no melanocytes at all in the patch. A biopsy shows melanocytes present in albinism and missing in vitiligo.

tricks.label: Bone, eye, or skin first
tricks.text: Fractures with blue sclerae point to type I collagen (osteogenesis imperfecta). Tall with a displaced lens points to fibrillin (Marfan). Stretchy skin and bad scars point to Ehlers-Danlos.

highYield: Albinism: normal melanocyte number, little or no melanin, classically tyrosinase loss; high risk of squamous and basal cell carcinoma.
Nystagmus and low visual acuity are common in oculocutaneous albinism.
Partial albinism, giant neutrophil granules, recurrent staphylococcal infections, and neuropathy: Chediak-Higashi (LYST).
Classic Ehlers-Danlos: type V collagen; vascular type: type III collagen; kyphoscoliotic type: lysyl hydroxylase.
Young adult with sudden colon perforation or arterial rupture and thin, bruised skin: vascular Ehlers-Danlos.
Lens subluxation and aortic root dilation point to Marfan, not Ehlers-Danlos.
pitfalls: Both scurvy and kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos impair collagen hydroxylation, but scurvy is acquired and adds perifollicular hemorrhage and gum disease.
Ocular albinism is X-linked; oculocutaneous albinism is autosomal recessive.
Joint hypermobility occurs in Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan, and osteogenesis imperfecta, so use skin, lens, and fractures to separate them.
Albinism raises nonmelanoma skin cancer risk; do not assume the main risk is pigmented melanoma.

dumps.p: Draw collagen synthesis from gene to cross-linked fibril. Mark the step that fails in each type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and in osteogenesis imperfecta.
l: Translation of alpha chains with glycine every third residue
Hydroxylation of proline and lysine (vitamin C dependent)
Kyphoscoliotic EDS: lysyl hydroxylase deficiency
Triple helix forms and procollagen is secreted
Procollagen peptidases cleave the ends outside the cell
Lysyl oxidase (copper dependent) cross-links fibrils
Classic EDS: type V collagen; vascular EDS: type III collagen
Osteogenesis imperfecta: type I collagen

flows.title: Melanin synthesis and transfer
steps: Tyrosine enters the melanosome of the melanocyte
Tyrosinase hydroxylates tyrosine to DOPA
Tyrosinase oxidizes DOPA to dopaquinone
Dopaquinone is converted to eumelanin or pheomelanin
Mature melanosomes pass through dendrites to neighboring keratinocytes
Melanin caps keratinocyte nuclei and absorbs UV

flows.title: Collagen synthesis
steps: Pro-alpha chains with Gly-X-Y repeats are made in the rough ER
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases hydroxylate residues (vitamin C needed)
Selected hydroxylysine residues are glycosylated
Three chains wind into a procollagen triple helix
Procollagen is secreted; peptidases cut the propeptides to form tropocollagen
Tropocollagen molecules self-assemble into fibrils
Lysyl oxidase (copper dependent) cross-links fibrils into strong fibers

summary: This unit covers common growths on the skin and mouth, from harmless (seborrheic keratosis, cysts, lipoma, hemangiomas) to premalignant (actinic keratosis, dysplastic nevi, leukoplakia). The exam asks you to recognize the lesion, explain what it can become, and spot skin signs that announce a hidden cancer.

points: UV-induced keratinocyte dysplasia on sun-exposed skin (face, scalp, ears, dorsal hands) in older fair-skinned adults.
Rough, sandpaper-like scaly papules, often easier to feel than to see.
Histology: atypia in the lower epidermis, parakeratosis, and solar elastosis (sun-damaged blue-gray dermal elastic tissue).
A small fraction progress to squamous cell carcinoma; many lesions mean high cumulative UV.
notes.why: UVB is absorbed directly by DNA and forms pyrimidine dimers; when these are not repaired, they leave C to T signature mutations, often in TP53. Keratinocytes with mutant p53 escape UV-induced apoptosis and expand as a clone starting in the basal layer, which is why atypia begins low in the epidermis. Faulty maturation leaves nuclei in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis), giving the rough scale, while chronic UV damage to dermal elastic fibers produces solar elastosis. Atypia through part of the epidermis is dysplasia; atypia through its full thickness is squamous cell carcinoma in situ.

points: Larger than common nevi (often over 5 mm), with irregular borders and variable pigment.
Biopsy: cytologic atypia plus architectural atypia (bridging nests, lentiginous growth).
A single dysplastic nevus rarely becomes melanoma; many of them mark a person at high melanoma risk.
Familial cases (familial atypical multiple mole melanoma) carry CDKN2A (p16) mutations and need close skin surveillance.
notes.why: Most nevi begin with an activating BRAF or NRAS mutation that drives a burst of melanocyte growth, after which the cells enter oncogene-induced senescence, which keeps a common nevus small and stable. Dysplastic nevi show disordered architecture and nuclear atypia, reflecting extra genetic changes that partly escape this brake. CDKN2A encodes p16, which inhibits CDK4 and CDK6 and keeps Rb active; inherited loss weakens senescence and the G1 checkpoint, so these families develop many atypical nevi and melanomas, often in normal-looking skin as well as in nevi.

points: Seborrheic keratosis: benign epidermal growth of older adults; tan to brown, waxy, stuck-on plaque.
Histology: basaloid cells with horn cysts; many carry FGFR3 activating mutations.
Leser-Trélat sign: sudden eruption of many seborrheic keratoses, a marker of internal cancer, classically gastric adenocarcinoma.
Acanthosis nigricans: velvety dark plaques in the neck and axillae; usually insulin resistance (obesity, type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome), rarely gastric adenocarcinoma.
Dermatomyositis in an adult: look for ovarian, lung, and GI cancers.
Paraneoplastic pemphigus: severe oral erosions with lymphoma or other lymphoid neoplasm.
notes.why: Seborrheic keratoses are clonal epidermal growths in which activating FGFR3 or PIK3CA mutations drive keratinocyte proliferation without the atypia of a cancer. Paraneoplastic skin signs come from tumor-derived growth factors; TGF-alpha from gastric adenocarcinoma acting on the EGF receptor of keratinocytes is one proposed cause of eruptive seborrheic keratoses and malignant acanthosis nigricans. In the common insulin-resistant form of acanthosis nigricans, high insulin activates IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts, causing papillomatosis and hyperkeratosis. Paraneoplastic pemphigus results from antibodies against plakin proteins and desmogleins, set off by the underlying lymphoid tumor.

points: Epidermal inclusion cyst: lined by stratified squamous epithelium with a granular layer, filled with laminated keratin; often has a central punctum.
A ruptured inclusion cyst triggers a foreign body giant cell reaction and becomes red and painful.
Trichilemmal (pilar) cyst: on the scalp, no granular layer, filled with dense compact keratin.
Lipoma: soft, mobile, painless mass of mature adipocytes; the most common soft tissue tumor of adults.
notes.why: An epidermal inclusion cyst forms when surface or infundibular epidermis becomes trapped in the dermis and keeps maturing normally, so it keeps a granular layer and sheds flaky, laminated keratin into the lumen. A trichilemmal cyst comes from the outer root sheath of the follicle isthmus, which keratinizes abruptly without a granular layer and makes dense, compact keratin. Keratin is highly irritating once it leaves its epithelial lining, so rupture provokes a foreign body giant cell reaction. Lipomas are benign clonal growths of mature fat cells, so they look and feel like normal fat but are encapsulated.

points: Infantile hemangioma: appears in the first weeks of life, grows for months, then slowly involutes over years.
Cherry hemangioma: small bright red papules on the trunk of older adults; benign.
Pyogenic granuloma: rapidly growing, friable red nodule that bleeds easily; common on gums in pregnancy and after minor trauma.
Port-wine stain: capillary malformation present at birth that persists and darkens; in the V1 facial distribution it suggests Sturge-Weber syndrome (leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, glaucoma).
notes.why: Vascular lesions divide into tumors, which grow by endothelial proliferation, and malformations, which are errors in vessel development that grow only in proportion to the child. Infantile hemangioma is a true tumor of GLUT1-positive endothelial cells with a growth phase in the first months and slow involution over years. Pyogenic granuloma is a reactive lobular capillary proliferation driven by trauma or pregnancy hormones, which explains its rapid growth and easy bleeding. A port-wine stain is a capillary malformation, and in Sturge-Weber syndrome a somatic GNAQ mutation affects the same embryonic vascular field in the face, leptomeninges, and eye, causing seizures and glaucoma.

points: Leukoplakia: white plaque that cannot be scraped off; tobacco and alcohol; may show dysplasia and can progress to squamous cell carcinoma, so biopsy it.
Oral hairy leukoplakia: corrugated white plaque on the lateral tongue, EBV, seen in HIV; cannot be scraped off; not premalignant.
Thrush (Candida): white curd-like plaques that scrape off and leave a red base.
notes.why: The scrape test separates an organism sitting on the surface from a change in the epithelium itself. Candida grows on top of the mucosa as pseudohyphae mixed with shed cells, so it wipes off and leaves inflamed red mucosa. Leukoplakia is thickened, keratinized epithelium, often from tobacco carcinogens that can cause dysplasia, so it cannot be removed and needs a biopsy. Oral hairy leukoplakia is EBV replicating in the upper layers of tongue epithelium in immunosuppressed patients, which produces corrugated hyperkeratosis without dysplasia.

highYield: Rough scaly papules on the scalp of an older farmer: actinic keratosis, a precursor of squamous cell carcinoma.
Many large irregular moles plus family members with melanoma: dysplastic nevus syndrome with CDKN2A mutation.
Sudden crop of seborrheic keratoses with weight loss: Leser-Trélat sign of gastric adenocarcinoma.
Acanthosis nigricans is usually insulin resistance; think cancer when it appears suddenly in a thin older adult.
Rupture of an epidermal inclusion cyst produces foreign body giant cell inflammation.
Bleeding red gum nodule in a pregnant woman: pyogenic granuloma.
Port-wine stain in the V1 distribution with seizures: Sturge-Weber syndrome.
pitfalls: Seborrheic keratosis is benign even when dark; it looks stuck on rather than growing into the skin.
Most melanomas arise without a prior nevus; dysplastic nevi mark risk rather than serve as the usual precursor.
Epidermal inclusion cyst keeps a granular layer; trichilemmal cyst lacks one.
Oral hairy leukoplakia is EBV-related and not premalignant; leukoplakia can progress to cancer.

summary: This unit covers the three main skin cancers (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma) and cutaneous T cell lymphoma. The exam asks you to match the lesion and biopsy to the cancer, name its risk factors and molecular driver, and predict how likely it is to spread.

points: Most common skin cancer; UV-driven, on sun-exposed skin, especially the face and upper lip.
Driven by hedgehog pathway activation, usually loss of PTCH1 or activation of SMO; germline PTCH1 loss causes many early BCCs (Gorlin syndrome).
Pearly papule with telangiectasias and rolled borders; can ulcerate in the center (rodent ulcer).
Histology: nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction clefts from the stroma.
Invades and destroys locally; metastasis is rare.
notes.why: The hedgehog pathway is normally held off by PTCH1, which suppresses SMO until hedgehog ligand binds. Loss of PTCH1 or an activating SMO mutation releases SMO, so GLI transcription factors switch on proliferation genes continuously in basal-type cells. Tumor cells at the edge of each nest line up in a palisade, copying the normal basal layer, and shrinkage away from the stroma during processing creates retraction clefts. BCC grows in close dependence on its own stroma, which is the usual explanation for why it invades locally but rarely metastasizes.

points: Risk factors: cumulative UV, actinic keratosis, transplant immunosuppression, arsenic, HPV, xeroderma pigmentosum, and chronic scars or ulcers.
Squamous cell carcinoma arising in a burn scar, chronic ulcer, or draining sinus is a Marjolin ulcer.
Favors the lower lip and sun-exposed skin, because those sites get the most UV.
Scaly, crusted, or ulcerated nodule; histology shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.
Bowen disease is squamous cell carcinoma in situ: a red scaly plaque with full-thickness atypia and an intact basement membrane.
Keratoacanthoma: dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin plug that grows over weeks and can regress; it looks like well-differentiated SCC.
Metastasizes more often than BCC, especially from the lip, ear, scars, and in transplant recipients.
notes.why: Squamous cell carcinoma arises as UV-induced mutations (TP53 early, then others such as NOTCH1) accumulate in keratinocytes, so risk tracks lifetime UV dose and the most sun-exposed sites. Immune surveillance normally clears many of these clones; transplant immunosuppression removes that control and lets oncogenic HPV persist, raising SCC risk many-fold and making tumors more aggressive. Chronic scars and ulcers keep keratinocytes proliferating under inflammation for years, so mutations build up and Marjolin ulcers arise. The tumor imitates squamous differentiation, which is why it forms keratin pearls and intercellular bridges (desmosomes).

points: Risk: intense intermittent UV (blistering sunburns), fair skin, many or dysplastic nevi, family history, CDKN2A, and xeroderma pigmentosum.
Superficial spreading: most common; trunk and legs; long horizontal (radial) phase.
Nodular: grows down from the start, so it is often thick when found.
Lentigo maligna: slow-growing on chronically sun-damaged faces of older adults.
Acral lentiginous: palms, soles, and nail beds; not tied to UV; the most common type in people with dark skin.
Mucosal: oral, nasal, anorectal, and genital (vulvar or penile) mucosa; not UV-related; often found late.
notes.why: Melanoma on intermittently sun-exposed skin of the trunk and legs often carries BRAF V600E and is linked to blistering sunburns, while lentigo maligna tracks chronic cumulative sun on the face. Acral and mucosal melanomas arise where UV barely reaches and carry other drivers such as KIT mutations, so they occur in all skin types and are often found late. The subtypes also differ in growth direction: radial (sideways) spread keeps superficial spreading and lentigo maligna thin for a long time, while nodular melanoma grows down from the start.

points: Radial growth phase: cells spread within the epidermis and superficial dermis and cannot metastasize.
Vertical growth phase: a clone grows down into the dermis as an expanding nodule, reaching vessels and lymphatics, so metastasis becomes possible.
Breslow thickness (mm from the granular layer to the deepest tumor cell) is the key prognostic factor in localized melanoma.
Ulceration and high mitotic rate also worsen prognosis.
Immunostains: S-100 (sensitive), HMB-45 and Melan-A (more specific melanocytic markers).
notes.why: In the radial growth phase, melanoma cells cannot yet survive and grow as a mass in the dermis, so they spread sideways and do not reach vessels. The vertical growth phase marks a clone that forms an expanding dermal nodule, invades lymphatics and blood vessels, and can metastasize. Breslow thickness measures how deep that clone has gone, so it estimates contact with vessels and best predicts survival in localized disease, with ulceration and a high mitotic rate adding risk. S-100 is sensitive but nonspecific, while HMB-45 and Melan-A detect melanosome proteins and are more specific for melanocytes.

points: Cutaneous lymphoma of CD4 T cells in older adults.
Moves through patch, plaque, and tumor stages over years.
Biopsy: atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform (folded) nuclei in the epidermis, forming Pautrier microabscesses.
Sézary syndrome: the leukemic form with generalized erythroderma and circulating Sézary cells.
notes.why: Mycosis fungoides is a clonal malignancy of skin-homing CD4 memory T cells that carry homing receptors such as cutaneous lymphocyte antigen and CCR4, so they enter the epidermis (epidermotropism) and cluster there as Pautrier microabscesses. The clone expands slowly from patch to plaque to tumor as it grows less dependent on the skin. When the malignant cells circulate in large numbers, the disease becomes Sézary syndrome, with erythroderma and blood cells that have cerebriform nuclei.

tricks.label: ABCDE of melanoma
tricks.text: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolution (change over time).

tricks.label: Upper lip basal, lower lip squamous
tricks.text: BCC classically sits on the upper lip and central face. SCC classically sits on the lower lip, which takes more direct sun.

tricks.label: Depth decides melanoma
tricks.text: A melanoma that stays flat (radial phase) cannot spread. Once it grows down (vertical phase), Breslow thickness tells you how dangerous it is.

highYield: Pearly papule with telangiectasias on the nose: basal cell carcinoma; palisading basaloid nests; rarely metastasizes.
Gorlin syndrome: germline PTCH1 loss with many early basal cell carcinomas.
Kidney transplant recipient with multiple scaly nodules: squamous cell carcinoma.
Ulcer that turns into a growing mass in an old burn scar: Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma).
Breslow thickness is the single most important prognostic factor for localized melanoma.
Dark streak under a nail or a lesion on the sole: acral lentiginous melanoma.
Itchy scaly patches for years, then plaques, with Pautrier microabscesses: mycosis fungoides; erythroderma with circulating cerebriform cells is Sézary syndrome.
pitfalls: Keratoacanthoma and well-differentiated SCC look alike; rapid growth over weeks and spontaneous regression favor keratoacanthoma.
Bowen disease is in situ SCC, so it has not yet invaded the dermis.
S-100 is sensitive but not specific; HMB-45 and Melan-A are more specific for melanocytes.
Acral and mucosal melanoma are not UV-driven, so they occur on palms, soles, nail beds, and mucosa that get little or no sun.
Melanoma is the most deadly skin cancer, but BCC is the most common.

SCC histology: keratin pearls and intercellular bridges; more metastasis than BCC

summary: This unit covers skin infections and infection-linked skin diseases: bacterial (impetigo, cellulitis, MRSA, wound and bite infections), fungal (candidiasis, tinea), viral (warts, molluscum, herpes, childhood rashes), mycobacterial, toxin-mediated, and parasitic. The exam gives you the setting and the lesion and asks for the organism, its virulence factor, or the complication to expect.

points: Four steps: follicular hyperkeratinization, androgen-driven sebum, Cutibacterium acnes growth, and inflammation.
Comedones are noninflamed plugs (open blackheads, closed whiteheads); papules, pustules, and nodules are inflamed and can scar.
Worse with hyperandrogenism (polycystic ovary syndrome) and glucocorticoids.
notes.why: Androgens enlarge sebaceous glands at puberty and raise sebum output, while abnormal keratinization of the follicular infundibulum makes corneocytes stick together and plug the follicle (a microcomedone). The sealed, lipid-rich follicle favors anaerobic Cutibacterium acnes, which breaks triglycerides into irritating free fatty acids and activates innate immunity through toll-like receptor 2. Rupture of the distended follicle spills keratin, sebum, and bacteria into the dermis, producing inflamed papules, pustules, nodules, and scars.

points: Folliculitis (inside the follicle), furuncle (deep follicular abscess), carbuncle (several furuncles joined, with draining sinuses); mostly Staphylococcus aureus. Related pus collections: skin abscess (usually S aureus) and pilonidal abscess in the sacrococcygeal cleft around trapped hair.
Hot tub folliculitis: Pseudomonas aeruginosa from poorly chlorinated water; itchy pustules where the swimsuit sat.
Nonbullous impetigo: honey-colored crusts around the nose and mouth in children; S aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.
Bullous impetigo: S aureus exfoliative toxin cuts desmoglein 1 and splits the granular layer.
MRSA: mecA on SCCmec encodes PBP2a, which does not bind beta-lactams; anterior nares are the main reservoir.
Community MRSA: Panton-Valentine leukocidin, recurrent abscesses in athletes, prisons, military, and injection drug use; hospital MRSA: devices, surgery, dialysis, more drug resistance.
notes.why: Staphylococcus aureus colonizes the anterior nares and enters through hair follicles and breaks in the skin, and the depth of infection names the lesion. Its exfoliative toxins are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein 1, which is why bullous impetigo splits high in the epidermis, at the same level as pemphigus foliaceus. Methicillin resistance comes from mecA, which encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams, so cell wall synthesis continues in the presence of the drug. Panton-Valentine leukocidin forms pores in neutrophil membranes and kills them, contributing to the necrotic abscesses of community MRSA.

points: Erysipelas: upper dermis and superficial lymphatics; raised, sharply demarcated, bright red; usually S pyogenes.
Cellulitis: deep dermis and subcutaneous fat; ill-defined warm red borders; S pyogenes or S aureus.
Portals of entry: tinea pedis fissures, wounds, ulcers, insect bites, lymphedema, and venous stasis.
Complications: abscess, lymphangitis (red streaks), bacteremia, and necrotizing fasciitis.
Necrotizing fasciitis: pain out of proportion to the exam, crepitus, rapid spread along fascial planes; surgical emergency.
Erythema nodosum: septal panniculitis without vasculitis; tender red nodules on the shins that heal without scarring.
Erythema nodosum triggers: strep infection, sarcoidosis, TB, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, IBD, and pregnancy.
notes.why: Streptococcus pyogenes spreads through tissue using hyaluronidase, streptokinase, and DNases, and the depth it reaches sets the appearance: erysipelas involves superficial dermal lymphatics and has a raised sharp edge, while cellulitis in the deeper dermis and fat has indistinct borders. In necrotizing fasciitis, organisms and toxins spread along the fascia and thrombose the vessels that supply the overlying skin, so deep tissue dies before the surface changes and pain exceeds the visible findings. Erythema nodosum is a hypersensitivity reaction centered on the septa between fat lobules, triggered by antigens from infection, sarcoidosis, IBD, or pregnancy, and it heals without scarring because the lobules themselves are spared.

points: Candidiasis: beefy red intertriginous plaques with satellite pustules; candidal diaper rash involves the skin folds, irritant diaper rash spares them.
Candida risk: diabetes, antibiotics, glucocorticoids (including inhaled), HIV, infancy, dentures; chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis points to a T cell (Th17) defect.
Tinea (dermatophytes: Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) is named by site; corporis has a scaly annular border with central clearing.
Tinea versicolor is Malassezia, a yeast, not a dermatophyte: hypo or hyperpigmented trunk macules in hot humid weather.

Warts (HPV): common (hands), plantar (soles), flat (face, shins), and anogenital condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6 and 11); histology shows papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and koilocytes; extensive warts suggest T cell immunodeficiency.
Molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus): firm, flesh-colored, umbilicated dome papules spread by contact, autoinoculation, and sex; self-limited in children, extensive in HIV.
Herpes simplex: herpes labialis, genital herpes, herpetic whitlow (finger), and eczema herpeticum on atopic skin.
Zoster: painful dermatomal vesicles, often followed by postherpetic neuralgia in older adults; Ramsay Hunt syndrome (geniculate ganglion) adds facial palsy and ear vesicles.
notes.why: Dermatophytes digest keratin, so they live only in the dead keratinized layers (stratum corneum, hair, nails) and spread outward in a ring while the host response clears the center. Th17 cells and IL-17 normally control Candida at skin and mucosal surfaces, so Th17 defects cause chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. HPV infects basal keratinocytes and replicates as the cells mature, producing koilocytes and papillomatosis, and cell-mediated immunity clears it, so warts multiply in T cell deficiency. HSV and VZV stay latent in sensory ganglia and reactivate along nerves, so recurrences return to the same site or a single dermatome.

points: Needle stick risk: hepatitis B highest (about 30% if the source is HBeAg positive), then hepatitis C (about 2%), then HIV (about 0.3%); risk rises with a hollow-bore blood-filled needle, deep injury, and high source viral load.
Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin (lecithinase) breaks cell membranes, causing gas gangrene with myonecrosis and crepitus.
Clostridium tetani in a puncture wound makes tetanospasmin, which travels to the CNS and blocks GABA and glycine release from inhibitory interneurons, causing spastic paralysis and trismus.

Bacillus anthracis: protective antigen carries edema factor (adenylate cyclase, raises cAMP) and lethal factor (a protease that kills macrophages) into cells; a polypeptide (D-glutamate) capsule resists phagocytosis; cutaneous anthrax is a painless papule that becomes a black eschar with marked edema.
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome: young children; exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1 in the granular layer; mucosa spared.
Toxic epidermal necrolysis: drug-triggered full-thickness epidermal necrosis with mucosal involvement.
notes.why: Needle stick transmission tracks how much virus the inoculated blood carries: HBV circulates at very high titers, HCV at intermediate levels, and HIV at lower levels, which explains the falling risks. Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin is a phospholipase C that hydrolyzes lecithin in cell membranes, killing muscle and red cells, while fermentation releases gas into tissue. Tetanospasmin travels retrograde along motor axons to the spinal cord and cleaves synaptobrevin in inhibitory interneurons, so without glycine and GABA release, motor neurons fire unchecked. SSSS splits superficially at desmoglein 1 and spares mucosa, while TEN kills full-thickness keratinocytes through drug-specific cytotoxic T cells and involves mucosa.

points: Mycobacterium leprae grows best below core body temperature, so it favors skin, peripheral nerves, nose, and earlobes; it depends on host cells and cannot be grown in culture (armadillos and mouse footpads are used).
Tuberculoid leprosy: strong Th1 response, few bacilli, few hypopigmented anesthetic plaques.
Lepromatous leprosy: Th2 response, many bacilli, diffuse nodules, leonine facies, symmetric nerve damage.
Scabies: Sarcoptes scabiei burrows in finger webs, wrists, and genitals; itch worse at night; crusted scabies with immunosuppression.
Head lice (nits on hair, children) and pubic lice (sexual contact); body lice live in clothing and spread Rickettsia prowazekii and Bartonella quintana; bedbug bites appear in linear clusters.
notes.why: Mycobacterium leprae grows best at about 30 °C (86 °F), so it favors cooler tissues such as skin, superficial nerves, nose, and earlobes. Its clinical form depends on the host T cell response: a Th1 response (IFN-gamma) activates macrophages to wall the organism into granulomas, giving few bacilli and localized lesions in tuberculoid leprosy, while a Th2 response fails to activate macrophages, so bacilli multiply freely inside them in lepromatous leprosy. Scabies itch is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to mites, eggs, and feces, which is why itch begins weeks after a first infestation, and unchecked mite growth in immunosuppression produces crusted scabies.

tricks.label: Rule of threes for needle sticks
tricks.text: Hepatitis B about 30% (HBeAg-positive source), hepatitis C about 2%, HIV about 0.3%. The order and the roughly tenfold steps are what to know.

tricks.label: Erysipelas is on the surface
tricks.text: Erysipelas sits high in the dermis, so its edge is raised and sharp. Cellulitis sits deep in the fat, so its edge fades out.

tricks.label: Folds tell you Candida
tricks.text: Candida loves warm moist folds, so a diaper rash in the creases with satellite spots is candidal. Irritant diaper rash hits skin touching the diaper and spares the creases.

tricks.label: Tetanus versus botulism
tricks.text: Tetanospasmin blocks inhibitory transmitters, so muscles go stiff (spastic). Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release, so muscles go limp (flaccid).

highYield: Honey-colored crusts around a child's mouth followed weeks later by cola-colored urine: impetigo then poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Recurrent abscesses in a wrestling team: community MRSA with Panton-Valentine leukocidin.
Red, swollen leg with pain far worse than it looks and crepitus: necrotizing fasciitis.
Tender shin nodules with bilateral hilar adenopathy: erythema nodosum with sarcoidosis.
Umbilicated papules on the face of an adult with HIV: molluscum contagiosum.
Cat bite with cellulitis by the next day: Pasteurella multocida; dog bite in an asplenic patient: Capnocytophaga.
Painless black eschar with large edema in a wool or hide worker: cutaneous anthrax.
Itchy burrows in the finger webs worse at night, with itchy family members: scabies.
pitfalls: Rheumatic fever follows strep pharyngitis only; glomerulonephritis can follow strep throat or skin infection.
Tinea versicolor is a yeast (Malassezia), not a dermatophyte, even though it is called tinea.
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome spares mucosa and splits high; toxic epidermal necrolysis involves mucosa and the full epidermis.
Varicella shows lesions in different stages at once; smallpox lesions are all at the same stage.
Erythema nodosum heals without ulcer or scar; a nodule that ulcerates on the calf suggests something else.

dumps.p: Draw a cross-section of skin from epidermis to muscle. Place impetigo, bullous impetigo, folliculitis, furuncle, erysipelas, cellulitis, and necrotizing fasciitis at the right depth and write the usual organism next to each.
l: Impetigo: superficial epidermis, S aureus or S pyogenes
Bullous impetigo: granular layer split by S aureus exfoliative toxin
Folliculitis in the follicle; furuncle deeper; carbuncle is several joined furuncles
Erysipelas: upper dermis and lymphatics, S pyogenes, sharp raised edge
Cellulitis: deep dermis and fat, S pyogenes or S aureus, ill-defined edge
Necrotizing fasciitis: along fascia, pain out of proportion, crepitus
Portal of entry such as tinea pedis fissures or wounds

dumps.p: Make a table with exposures down the left (cat or dog bite, dog bite without spleen, human bite, seawater, fish tank, rose thorn, soil-contaminated deep wound, puncture wound, needle stick) and write the organism and its key clue for each.
l: Cat or dog bite: Pasteurella multocida
Dog bite with asplenia: Capnocytophaga canimorsus
Human bite: Eikenella corrodens
Seawater: Vibrio vulnificus; fish tank: Mycobacterium marinum
Rose thorn: Sporothrix schenckii with lymphatic spread
Deep soil wound: C perfringens alpha toxin and gas gangrene
Puncture wound: C tetani, tetanospasmin blocks GABA and glycine release
Needle stick: hepatitis B over hepatitis C over HIV

flows.title: Acne vulgaris pathogenesis
steps: Androgens enlarge sebaceous glands and raise sebum output
Follicular hyperkeratinization plugs the infundibulum (microcomedone)
Sebum and keratin build up into open or closed comedones
Cutibacterium acnes multiplies and releases free fatty acids
Innate immune activation draws in neutrophils
The follicle ruptures into the dermis, forming papules, pustules, and nodules

flows.title: Tetanus pathogenesis
steps: Clostridium tetani spores germinate in an anaerobic puncture wound
Bacteria release tetanospasmin
Toxin enters motor nerve terminals and travels retrograde to the spinal cord
Toxin passes into inhibitory interneurons
Toxin cleaves synaptobrevin, blocking GABA and glycine release
Unopposed motor neuron firing causes trismus and spastic paralysis

flows.title: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxin disease
steps: Staphylococcus aureus releases exfoliative toxins
Toxin acts locally (bullous impetigo) or circulates (scalded skin syndrome)
The serine protease cleaves desmoglein 1
Keratinocytes separate in the granular layer
Superficial flaccid bullae and sloughing appear, sparing mucosa
